DISCUSSION
Basic synchro systems convert mechanical movement into an electrical signal which is then used to duplicate the mechanical movement at another location.

In its simplest form the synchro system consists of a transmitter and a receiver. They are electrically identical but slightly different mechanically. The receiver has a built-in mechanical damper to prevent back and forth oscillations (known as hunting) at the rotational position provided by the transmitter..
Both the transmitter and receiver incorporate a primary electrical winding on a movable rotor and three stationary secondary windings spaced 120
apart on the stator. The primary of both is energized with single phase AC voltage of 60 or 400Hz...

Depending upon the position of the rotor in the transmitter, voltage is induced in the transmitter's secondary stator windings. This voltage may be in or out of phase with the rotor winding due to the positional relationship between the rotor and each winding...

The voltage is applied to the counterpart stator windings of the receiver. The magnetic fields generated by the secondary windings and the rotor winding of the receiver causes the receiver rotor to position itself to the same rotational position as the rotor of the transmitter...

The basic synchro system as described thus far performs adequately provided high torque and positional correction is not required. The receiver rotor (TR) will follow the rotational positioning of the transmitter rotor...

Control Synchro Systems produce no torque, so they do not directly position the load. Instead they "control" the movement of the entire servo system through a series of amplifiers to position the load.....

In a Torque system or a Control system should positional correction be needed the correction is provided by another rotational transformer known as the Torque Differential Transmitter (TDX) or the Control Differential Transmitter (CDX)...
The most common application is navigational correction on ships, planes, and land vehicles and systems on motorized assemblies..zed assemblies..

The Torque/Control Differential Transmitter (TDX/CDX) incorporates three stator windings with 120
spacing just as with the Torque Transmitter and the Torque Receiver. The rotor, though, also has three windings, also spaced at 120

The input to the Torque/Control Differential Transmitter (TDX/CDX) is the output of the Torque/Control Transmitter (TX/CX) with the outputs of the transmitter windings connected to their counterpart windings on the TDX/CDX, S1 to S1, S2 to S2, and S3 to S3...

Electrical energy induced in the stator windings of the transmitter is fed to their counterpart differential transmitter windings. The resulting magnetic fields in the stator windings of the differential transmitter develop electrical energy in the three windings of the differential transmitter rotor...

The rotor of the differential transmitter receives mechanical position input from an external source. The positional relationship between the differential transmitter stator windings and rotor windings produces an output from the rotor windings, which is used for correction...

Always remember that both rotors mentioned thus far, on the Torque/Control Transmitter and the Torque/Control Differential Transmitter are not free to spin. Each receives positional input from a mechanical source and is held in position...

The output of the Torque/Control Differential Transmitter is taken from the three rotor windings and is supplied to the Torque Receiver or Control Transolver. The Torque Receiver performs the same function as with the simple synchro system...

The Torque Receiver (TR) has the same in-phase voltage applied to the rotor winding as the Torque Transmitter (TX). The Torque Receiver stator windings are no longer connected to the Torque Transmitter stator windings but instead to the Torque Differential Transmitter (TDX) ROTOR windings...
The Torque Differential Transmitter (TDX) allows full 360

rotation of the rotor just as with the Torque Transmitter (TX). In our example it allows the targeting of the other ship using a compass heading as the Torque Differential Transmitter automatically supplies the targeting corrections...
